topic: The Pi Collision: How Bouncing Blocks Reveal the World's Most Famous Constant
target_audience: Advanced high school students and undergraduate students with a basic understanding of physics.

sections.title: The Setup: A Strange Observation
sections.content: Introduce the physical scenario: A frictionless surface with a vertical wall on the left. A small block (mass m) sits still. A large block (mass M) comes from the right at a constant velocity. We count the total number of collisions (block-block and block-wall) until the blocks move away from each other forever.
sections.example: Imagine a tiny ant pushing a small 1kg block, while a giant robot pushes a massive 100kg block toward it. When the masses are equal, we count 3 collisions. When the big block is 100x heavier, we count 31 collisions.

sections.title: The Pattern Emerges
sections.content: Present the data for mass ratios of 100^n. As the mass ratio increases by powers of 100, the number of collisions perfectly matches the digits of Pi. This section uses a visual table and a 'counter' animation to highlight the correlation.
sections.example: Ratio 1:1 -> 3 collisions; Ratio 100:1 -> 31 collisions; Ratio 10,000:1 -> 314 collisions; Ratio 1,000,000:1 -> 3,141 collisions. The digits of π are literally appearing in the physics lab!

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Conservation Laws
sections.content: Introduce the two governing equations: Conservation of Momentum (linear) and Conservation of Energy (quadratic). Explain that the state of the system can be defined by the velocities of the two blocks (v and V).
sections.example: Visualize a graph where the x-axis is the small block's velocity and the y-axis is the large block's velocity. The Energy equation creates an ellipse: (1/2)mv² + (1/2)MV² = Const.

sections.title: The Geometric Transformation
sections.content: To simplify the math, we 'stretch' the coordinate system to turn the energy ellipse into a perfect circle. This makes every collision look like a simple reflection. Introduce the scaled velocity variables: x = v * sqrt(m) and y = V * sqrt(M).
sections.example: Think of it like looking at a tilted coin (ellipse) and rotating it until it looks like a perfect circle. In this new world, the physics becomes a game of 'Circle Billiards'.

sections.title: Mapping Collisions to Arcs
sections.content: Explain that each block-block collision and block-wall collision corresponds to a jump along the circle. Each jump covers a fixed angle θ. The total number of collisions is the number of times we can fit this angle into the circle's path before the trajectory points away from the wall.
sections.example: Visual: A laser pointer bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each 'thud' of the block is a 'flash' of light hitting the mirror edge. The angle θ is determined by the square root of the mass ratio.

sections.title: Closing the Loop: Why Pi?
sections.content: Final synthesis: Show that as mass M becomes much larger, the angle θ becomes tiny. The number of bounces N is approximately the total arc length (related to π) divided by the step size θ. This yields the digits of Pi with increasing precision.
sections.example: As the giant robot's block gets heavier and heavier, it’s like dividing a circle into millions of tiny slices. Counting those slices is exactly what we do when we calculate the circumference of a circle—leading us straight to 3.14159...
